title: The Battle of Vicksburg
summary: Follow Grant's 1863 march to Vicksburg along the Mississippi River, and see why taking the city split the Confederacy in two.
subject: History
time: About 59 minutes: 49 for the questions and 10 to write the answer. One question on its own takes 10–15
studentLogin: Not needed to explore the map

map.about: This map is set on the Mississippi River around Vicksburg in spring 1863. Five dark pins, labeled on the map, mark places on Grant's route, and a yellow pin marks Vicksburg. A railroad layer shows the lines in the region (it includes lines built after the war, and disappears when you zoom out). The Civil War Battlefields layer, off when the map opens, adds Civil War battles, including those around Vicksburg.

image.alt: The Mississippi River around Vicksburg, with five dark pins labeled with place names, a yellow pin at Vicksburg, and railroad lines.

layers.name: Key Places in the Union March to Vicksburg
layers.shows: Places on Grant's route in spring 1863, as dark pins labeled on the map: Miliken's Bend, New Carthage, Hard Times, Bruinsburg Bend and Edwards, plus a yellow pin at Vicksburg. No pop-ups.

layers.name: Railroads 1826 to 1911
layers.shows: Railroads built from 1826 to 1911, so it includes lines built after the war. They draw at the bookmark's view and disappear when zoomed out. Clicking a line opens a list of data fields, including In Operation By (the year); no question uses it.

compellingQuestion.en: Why did the Union need Vicksburg, and how did Grant take it?
compellingQuestion.es: ¿Por qué necesitaba la Unión a Vicksburg y cómo la tomó Grant?

questions.task: Open The Battle of Vicksburg bookmark. Vicksburg is the yellow pin. Look at where it sits on the Mississippi River. Find the railroad line and follow it east from Vicksburg to Jackson, Mississippi, the state capital, which is a basemap label (not a pin) just past the bookmark's east edge. Why would both sides want the city?

Point to the yellow pin at Vicksburg on the bend of the Mississippi River.
Point to the railroad line (thin and dark, with cross marks) running east from Vicksburg.
Drag the map east and follow the railroad from Vicksburg to the Jackson label on the basemap.
Ask: why would both sides want Vicksburg?

steps.es: Abre el marcador The Battle of Vicksburg (la batalla de Vicksburg).

steps.es: Arrastra el mapa hacia el este para encontrar Jackson, Misisipi, en el mapa base (la capital del estado, al este de Vicksburg).

ask.en: Why would both sides want Vicksburg?

answer.where: The Battle of Vicksburg bookmark; yellow pin at Vicksburg on a bend of the Mississippi; Railroads 1826 to 1911 layer, which already draws at the bookmark and disappears when zoomed out past about 1:1,500,000; Jackson is a label on the Modern Antique basemap about 40 miles east, just beyond the bookmark's east edge, so students drag the map to reach it.
answer.accept: Says Vicksburg sits on the river, so whoever held it controlled traffic on the Mississippi, and that its railroad linked the river to Jackson and the rest of the Confederacy, so it was both a river stronghold and a rail junction. Mentioning the bluffs or guns is extra, not on the map.

questions.task: Find the dark pins and put them in order along Grant's route: Milliken's Bend (spelled Miliken's Bend on the map, at the top edge of the bookmark's view), New Carthage, Hard Times, Bruinsburg Bend, then Edwards. Which side of the river is each on? Measure the straight-line distance from Milliken's Bend to Bruinsburg Bend.

ask.en: Which side of the river is each place on? How far south of Milliken's Bend did Grant cross, and why did he not cross at Vicksburg itself?
ask.es: ¿De qué lado del río está cada lugar? ¿A qué distancia al sur de Milliken's Bend cruzó Grant, y por qué no cruzó en la propia Vicksburg?

fill.en: Measure the distance from Milliken's Bend to Bruinsburg Bend: ________ miles
fill.es: Mide la distancia de Milliken's Bend a Bruinsburg Bend: ________ millas

answer.where: Key Places in the Union March to Vicksburg pins, read against the river and the basemap state labels: Milliken's Bend, New Carthage and Hard Times are on the west (Louisiana) bank; Bruinsburg Bend and Edwards are on the east (Mississippi) side. Measure tool, Milliken's Bend pin to Bruinsburg Bend pin: about 33 miles in a straight line (accept 31 to 36).
answer.accept: Notices that Vicksburg's pin sits on the river between Milliken's Bend (north) and Bruinsburg Bend (south), so Grant could not cross right at the city; he marched down the far bank, out of reach of the city, crossed well to the south, then turned back toward Vicksburg from the east (Edwards).

questions.task: Turn on Civil War Battlefields in Map layers and click the diamonds between Bruinsburg Bend and Vicksburg, and east toward Jackson. Put the battles in order by date from the pop-ups.

Click the Vicksburg diamond and read its two dates.
Ask: in what order were the battles fought, and which way did Grant's army move?

ask.en: Which battles were fought between Bruinsburg Bend, Vicksburg and Jackson? List them in order by date. Did Grant go straight to Vicksburg?
ask.es: ¿Qué batallas se libraron entre Bruinsburg Bend, Vicksburg y Jackson? Ordénalas por fecha. ¿Fue Grant directamente a Vicksburg?

answer.where: Civil War Battlefields pop-ups: the name is in bold and the dates below it. Grand Gulf (April 29, 1863), on the river just north of Bruinsburg, is the Union navy's failed attack before the crossing; accept it if students include it.

table.caption: Battles of Grant's Vicksburg campaign, from the pop-ups

answer.accept: The battles in date order (see the table). No: after Port Gibson the dates lead east to Raymond and Jackson (May 12 and 14), then back west through Champion Hill and Big Black River Bridge (May 16 and 17) to Vicksburg (May 18), so Grant reached Vicksburg from the east.

ask.en: When did Port Hudson end? Which states lie west of the river? What could the Union control once Vicksburg and Port Hudson had both fallen?
ask.es: ¿Cuándo terminó Port Hudson? ¿Qué estados quedan al oeste del río? ¿Qué pudo controlar la Unión una vez que cayeron Vicksburg y Port Hudson?

answer.where: Civil War Battlefields pop-up for Port Hudson: May 21, 1863 – July 9, 1863. Vicksburg pop-up: May 18, 1863 – July 4, 1863. Basemap state labels west of the river: Louisiana (most of it), Arkansas, Texas (and Missouri further north, Union side).
answer.accept: Port Hudson surrendered on July 9, 1863, five days after Vicksburg. Names Louisiana, Arkansas and Texas west of the river and says the Union then controlled the whole Mississippi, so those Confederate states were cut off from the rest of the Confederacy and the river was open to Union ships and closed to Confederate supplies.

final.teacher: Students answer with evidence from at least two places on the map. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, Grant's route sketched on the map (sketches are not saved, so students should screenshot or describe them), or a short talk using the map.

student.en: Answer the big question. Describe Grant's route in order, naming at least three places from the map.
student.es: Responde la pregunta central. Describe la ruta de Grant en orden y nombra al menos tres lugares del mapa.

objectives: Locate Vicksburg on the Mississippi River and follow the railroad east to Jackson to explain why both sides wanted the city.
Put the key places on Grant's route in order, say which bank of the river each is on, and measure the distance from Milliken's Bend to Bruinsburg Bend.
List the battles of the Vicksburg campaign in date order from the Civil War Battlefields pop-ups.
Identify from the basemap which Confederate states lay west of the Mississippi and what the Union controlled once Vicksburg and Port Hudson had fallen.
Use evidence from at least two places on the map to explain why the Union needed Vicksburg and how Grant took it.
discussion: Grant marched his army down the far bank and crossed more than 30 miles south of the city. What on the map explains that choice, and what risks did it carry?
Between Port Gibson on May 1 and the start of the siege on May 18, the battles run east toward Jackson and then back west. Why might Grant have gone to Jackson first instead of straight to Vicksburg?

Zoomed out, the river runs from Memphis to the Gulf with Louisiana, Arkansas and Texas on the far side. How does the map help explain why Vicksburg's surrender, and not just Gettysburg, was a turning point of July 1863?

differentiation.support: Do question 2 together from the front, listing the five pins in order on the board, before students measure the distance themselves.
differentiation.stretch: Measure Vicksburg to Port Hudson and Vicksburg to Memphis, and ask how much of the river the Confederacy still held in spring 1863.

assessment.evidence: Strong answers use the yellow Vicksburg pin on the Mississippi and the railroad east to the Jackson basemap label, the dark Key Places pins in order (Milliken's Bend to Edwards) with Measure from Milliken's Bend to Bruinsburg Bend (about 33 miles), and dates from the Civil War Battlefields pop-ups (Port Gibson, May 1, 1863; Vicksburg, May 18, 1863 – July 4, 1863; Port Hudson, to July 9, 1863).
assessment.exemplar: The Union needed Vicksburg because it controlled the Mississippi River, and Grant took it by going around it. Vicksburg sits on a bend of the river, and a railroad runs east from it to Jackson, so it linked the river to the rest of the Confederacy. Grant did not cross at the city. He marched down the Louisiana side from Milliken's Bend to New Carthage and Hard Times, and crossed at Bruinsburg Bend, about 33 miles south in a straight line. Then he went east, not straight to Vicksburg. The battles were Port Gibson on May 1, Raymond on May 12, Jackson on May 14, Champion Hill on May 16 and Big Black River Bridge on May 17, 1863. The siege of Vicksburg lasted from May 18 to July 4. Port Hudson fell on July 9, so the Union held the whole river, and Louisiana, Arkansas and Texas were cut off.

beforeYouStart.en: In 1862, Union forces captured New Orleans and Memphis, two cities on the Mississippi River. Between the two, the Confederates still held part of the river, including the city of Vicksburg, Mississippi. In spring 1863, Union General Ulysses S. Grant set out to capture it.
beforeYouStart.es: En 1862, las fuerzas de la Unión tomaron Nueva Orleans y Memphis, dos ciudades a orillas del río Misisipi. Entre ambas, los confederados todavía controlaban parte del río, incluida la ciudad de Vicksburg, en Misisipi. En la primavera de 1863, el general de la Unión Ulysses S. Grant se propuso tomarla.

readingTheMap.en: The yellow pin is Vicksburg. Dark pins mark places on Grant's route, each with its name. City and state names, such as Jackson and Louisiana, are part of the basemap. Railroads are thin dark lines with short cross marks, like a track; they disappear if you zoom out too far, and they include lines built after the war. Civil War Battlefields is off when the map opens: turn it on in Map layers. Its diamonds mark battles, colored by who won: use the legend to read the result, because a battle's pop-up gives its name and dates but not the result.
readingTheMap.es: El alfiler amarillo es Vicksburg. Los alfileres oscuros marcan lugares de la ruta de Grant, cada uno con su nombre. Los nombres de ciudades y estados, como Jackson y Luisiana, forman parte del mapa base. Los ferrocarriles son líneas oscuras finas con pequeñas marcas transversales, como una vía; desaparecen si te alejas demasiado e incluyen líneas construidas después de la guerra. La capa Civil War Battlefields está desactivada al abrir el mapa: actívala en las capas del mapa (Map layers). Sus rombos marcan las batallas, con un color según quién ganó: usa la leyenda para saber el resultado, porque la ventana emergente de una batalla da su nombre y sus fechas, pero no el resultado.

reflection.en: Grant crossed the river well south of the city he wanted. What does that tell you about Vicksburg?
reflection.es: Grant cruzó el río muy al sur de la ciudad que quería tomar. ¿Qué te dice eso sobre Vicksburg?

teacherNotes.beforeClass: Start from The Battle of Vicksburg bookmark. Civil War Battlefields is off when the map opens; students turn it on for questions 3 and 4. Jackson, Mississippi, is a basemap label, not a pin.

misconceptions.claim: Grant attacked Vicksburg straight across the river.
misconceptions.response: The key places show he marched south on the Louisiana side and crossed at Bruinsburg, well south of the city.

misconceptions.claim: Vicksburg fell in a single battle.
misconceptions.response: Its pop-up gives May 18 to July 4, 1863: a siege of about six weeks.

misconceptions.claim: Gettysburg was the only turning point of July 1863.
misconceptions.response: Vicksburg surrendered on July 4, 1863, the day after Gettysburg ended, and gave the Union the Mississippi.
